title: Chart switching and atlas overlap: where do charts cover and where do they fail?
summary: A curved space cannot always be labelled by one coordinate system. Several charts, each good on part of the space, cover it together, and a transition map converts between them wherever they overlap.

media.alt: Left: a circle surrounded by a teal arc and a dashed blue arc, two orange overlap arcs and two pink markers at the top and bottom poles, with a legend. Right: the hyperbola v = 1/u in orange with a dashed rose line at u = 0.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

read_the_figure.question: Where do charts cover and where do they fail?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: the circle S1 in the plane, with the two charts drawn as arcs slightly outside it (radius 1.1 and 1.2) so you can see them; orange marks the overlap; pink markers are the poles N (top) and S (bottom). Right: chart A coordinate u on the horizontal axis, chart B coordinate v vertical, both -4 to 4.
look_at: Which parts of the circle are covered by both charts?
What happens at each pole? Each chart misses exactly one pole.
What is the transition map and what does it do near u = 0?
Is the transition map smooth, with a smooth inverse, on the overlap?
as_drawn: The charts are u = x/(1+y) and v = x/(1-y). The first is undefined at the south pole (0, -1) and the second at the north pole (0, 1).

The left legend says chart A 'fails at N' and chart B 'fails at S'. By the formulas it is the other way round: x/(1+y) is fine at N (it gives 0) and fails at S. The right panel is consistent with the formulas: u = 0 is the north pole, where chart B fails and v = 1/u blows up. Read the formulas, not the left legend.
Arcs are offset radially for visibility; the charts really live on the circle itself. The vertical axis of the right panel is cut at plus and minus 4, so the divergence is off the picture.
read_the_figure.proves: That two charts cover the circle (each misses one point) and that the transition map v = 1/u on the overlap is smooth with smooth inverse: the defining properties of an atlas. A drawing cannot prove smoothness; the formula does.
if_wrong: No overlap region marked: you cannot see where conversion is possible.
Unlabelled pole markers: you cannot tell which chart fails where.
Charts drawn on top of each other with no offset: they are indistinguishable.

terms.meaning: A space that looks like ordinary flat space near each of its points (a circle, a sphere).
A one-to-one labelling of part of the manifold by coordinates.
A collection of charts that together cover the whole manifold.
The region covered by two charts at once.
The function that converts the coordinates of one chart into the other on the overlap.
A point where a chart fails because of the labelling, not because the space is bad there.

remember: One chart rarely covers a curved space; use an atlas.
A transition map must be smooth with a smooth inverse on every overlap.
Each chart should fail only where another chart works.
A failure of coordinates is not a failure of the space.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Arcs show chart domains; their colour or dash separates charts. Orange arcs show where both are valid. Markers name the points where a chart fails. In the right panel position encodes the two coordinates of the same point, and the curve is the conversion rule.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: No single coordinate covers the whole circle: x/(1+y) breaks at one pole and x/(1-y) at the other. The circle is perfectly smooth at both poles; only the labelling breaks. Two charts, each breaking at a different point, cover everything. On the overlap, the conversion v = 1/u says exactly how to translate coordinates, and it is smooth.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A drawing with offset arcs suggests charts live off the space. A transition plot cut at plus and minus 4 hides infinity. Swapped labels (as in the left legend of this render) turn a correct diagram into a wrong lesson. And a transition curve shows only the conversion, not whether orientation is kept.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Marking the overlap shows where conversion is possible; marking each failure point shows the cover is complete. Labelling the boundary tells you exactly where the transition map blows up: u = 0 on the right matches a pole on the left.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For a sphere use latitude-longitude (fails at poles) and stereographic charts, and colour the distortion with ellipses (F2.7). For a diagram of the logic only, draw two overlapping discs with the transition arrow between them. For numerical use, store a transition table.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour the circle by the value of u on chart A and by v on chart B and plot both, so the reader sees u and v run in opposite directions near the poles; add a third chart to show redundancy.

steps.title: The two charts and their transition
steps.note: The product uses x^2 = 1 - y^2 on the circle. Checked at sample points: uv = 1 everywhere except at the two poles, where a chart is undefined.

steps.title: Smoothness of the transition
steps.note: The derivative never vanishes and the inverse is the same function, so the conversion is a diffeomorphism on the overlap u not equal to 0. This is the condition that makes the two charts a smooth atlas.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the formulas and the right panel: (1) which pole does each chart miss? (2) What is v when u = 2? (3) What happens to v as u approaches 0?

solution.text: u = x/(1+y) is undefined at y = -1, the south pole; v = x/(1-y) is undefined at y = 1, the north pole. (The render's left legend has these swapped.)
The orange curve at u = 2 is at v = 0.5.
v grows without bound: u = 0 is the north pole, where chart B has no value. The orange branches leave the picture beyond plus and minus 4.

worked.answer: Chart A misses S, chart B misses N; v = 1/u on the overlap; the transition blows up at the pole that chart B cannot label.

analyze.q: The left legend of the figure says chart A fails at N, but the formulas say S. How would you detect such an error without the formulas?
analyze.hint: Look at what happens to u near each pole.

checks.q: Why can't a circle be covered by one chart?
checks.hint: Consider the end points of an interval.
checks.answer: A single chart maps an open interval to the circle; covering the whole loop with one smooth one-to-one coordinate would need the ends to meet. At least two overlapping charts are needed.

checks.q: A point has chart-A coordinate u = 0.25. What is its chart-B coordinate?
A chart 'fails' at a pole. Is the circle singular there?
checks.answer: No: the circle is perfectly smooth there; only the coordinate labelling breaks. The other chart handles the point.
